sections.heading: How a dollar of cloud capex becomes profit (and when)
bullets: When a cloud provider buys a server, the purchase is not an expense that quarter — it becomes an asset on the balance sheet, and accounting spreads its cost over an assumed useful life (say six years) as annual depreciation

That timing gap creates the signature pattern of a buildout: cash pours out immediately, so free cash flow collapses, while reported profit stays healthy — because only one-sixth of each server's cost hits the income statement per year

The useful-life assumption is a quiet profit lever: stretching servers from four years to six cuts annual depreciation and lifts reported margins with no operational change — which is why analysts scrutinize it during AI buildouts

The bet only works if the asset earns for its whole assumed life: a chip generation that obsoletes hardware in three years turns remaining book value into a write-off — a depreciation schedule is really a demand forecast in disguise

sections.heading: ASICs vs GPUs: why a cloud builds its own chips
bullets: A GPU (graphics processing unit) is a general-purpose parallel engine that can run almost any AI workload; an ASIC (application-specific integrated circuit) hardwires one job — say, training neural networks — trading flexibility for efficiency at that single job

The economics only close at hyperscale: designing a modern chip costs hundreds of millions, so you must deploy hundreds of thousands of units to amortize it — which is why only the largest clouds and labs attempt custom silicon

The payoff is dual: better price-performance per watt on your own workloads, and negotiating leverage against the dominant GPU vendor — every credible in-house chip quietly lowers the price of the chips you still buy

Custom silicon needs an anchor customer to absorb volume: a frontier lab committing gigawatts of capacity to the in-house chip gives the program the guaranteed utilization that justifies funding the next design generation

sections.heading: How a corporate PPA actually works
bullets: A power purchase agreement (PPA) is a long-term contract — often 10 to 20 years — to buy a project's electricity at an agreed price; the developer needs that creditworthy commitment to convince banks to finance construction at all

Most corporate PPAs are 'virtual': no electrons flow to the buyer — the contract is a fixed-price swap where the project sells into the wholesale market and the two parties settle the difference between market price and the agreed strike price

The buyer typically keeps the renewable energy certificates (RECs) — tradable proof that one megawatt-hour of clean power was generated — which is what lets a company claim its consumption is renewable-matched

'Additionality' is the quality test: a purchase counts most when it causes a new project to be built rather than claiming credit for existing generation — serious buyers sign PPAs with unbuilt projects, accepting development risk to create new supply

sections.heading: Plugging into a power plant: the co-location cost-shifting fight
bullets: Behind-the-meter co-location wires a giant new load directly to an existing power plant, in front of the grid connection — attractive because it captures firm power in months instead of waiting years for new transmission to be studied and built

The objection is cost-shifting: the plant used to serve everyone, and diverting its output off the shared grid can leave remaining customers paying more for transmission and backup capacity that the departing load still implicitly relies on

Deciding who pays for shared grid infrastructure when a big customer bypasses it is exactly what the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) exists for — and a landmark docket rejected an uncompensated behind-the-meter arrangement, setting the national template

The workaround is front-of-meter: the plant sells through the grid under a conventional PPA, the load pays its allocated share of grid costs, and the deal becomes transparent to regulators — slower and costlier, but durable

sections.heading: Warehouse robotics: AI's most industrial application
bullets: A fulfillment robot decomposes into the classic AI stack: perception (what is around me), motion planning (how do I get there without collisions), and manipulation (how do I grasp this item) — each genuinely hard in cluttered, constantly changing spaces

The architectural insight is goods-to-person: instead of humans walking miles of aisles, drive units carry whole shelves to stationary pickers — cutting travel time, densifying storage, and converting a warehouse into a solvable routing problem

Fleet orchestration is the invisible layer: thousands of robots sharing one floor need real-time traffic control — an optimization system continuously assigning tasks and routes, closer to air-traffic control than to any single robot's intelligence

Robotics closes the AI loop economically: the same company that sells AI compute uses AI to attack its largest operating cost — fulfillment labor per package — making the warehouse a proving ground for machine perception at industrial reliability

sections.heading: Reading a conglomerate: segments, mix, and the engine inside
bullets: A conglomerate reports by segment — separate revenue and operating income for each business — because a company-wide average hides everything: a thin-margin retail giant can contain a high-margin cloud business that produces most of the actual profit

Operating margin per segment is the tell: divide each segment's operating income by its revenue and compare — a business earning 35-40 cents per dollar sitting beside one earning 3-5 cents shows you which engine funds the buildout

Mix shift explains 'improving' profitability without any business changing: when the high-margin segment grows faster, the blended margin rises mechanically — always ask whether margins actually improved or the mix just moved

Sum-of-the-parts valuation follows: analysts value each segment as if it were standalone — the cloud like a software company, retail like a retailer — and add them up, which is why changes in segment disclosure alone can re-rate a stock

flashcards.q: Why doesn't buying a billion dollars of servers reduce reported profit that quarter?
flashcards.a: Capital expenditure becomes an asset, not an expense: the cost is spread over the server's assumed useful life as depreciation. Only that year's slice hits the income statement — so profit looks healthy even as cash pours out the door.

flashcards.q: Why does free cash flow collapse during an AI buildout while net income stays strong?
flashcards.a: Free cash flow subtracts capex the moment cash is spent; net income only subtracts depreciation, which spreads the same cost over years. A heavy buildout therefore shows the split personality of negative cash flow and record profits simultaneously.

flashcards.q: How can changing a server's assumed useful life change reported profit?
flashcards.a: Stretching the useful life from four years to six cuts each year's depreciation charge, lifting margins with no operational change. It's legitimate if hardware truly lasts longer — but if a new chip generation obsoletes gear early, the leftover book value becomes a write-off.

flashcards.q: What trade does an ASIC make versus a GPU?
flashcards.a: An application-specific integrated circuit hardwires one workload — like neural-network math — gaining efficiency and cost-per-operation while giving up the GPU's flexibility to run anything. It wins exactly when one workload is enormous, stable, and yours.

flashcards.q: Why can only hyperscalers justify designing their own AI chips?
flashcards.a: A chip program costs hundreds of millions before the first unit ships, so the design must amortize over hundreds of thousands of deployed units. Only a company with massive guaranteed internal demand — or an anchor customer committing gigawatts — clears that bar.

flashcards.q: How does an in-house chip pay off even on the chips a cloud still buys?
flashcards.a: It creates negotiating leverage: a credible alternative caps what the dominant GPU vendor can charge. The in-house program earns a return on every externally purchased chip through better pricing, even before its own units win workloads.

flashcards.q: How does a virtual PPA work if no electricity is ever delivered to the buyer?
flashcards.a: It's a fixed-price swap: the renewable project sells into the wholesale market, and the parties settle the difference between market price and the agreed strike. The buyer gets price certainty plus the renewable energy certificates; the developer gets bankable revenue to finance construction.

flashcards.q: What is additionality and why do serious clean-energy buyers insist on it?
flashcards.a: Additionality means the purchase caused new clean generation to be built, rather than claiming credit for plants that already existed. Signing a PPA with an unbuilt project — taking development risk — is what actually adds carbon-free supply to the grid.

flashcards.q: What is the cost-shifting objection to behind-the-meter co-location at a power plant?
flashcards.a: When a plant's output is diverted straight to one private load, remaining grid customers can end up paying more for the transmission and backup capacity the departing load still implicitly depends on. Whether that bypass is fairly compensated is a federal regulatory question — and the precedent went against uncompensated arrangements.

flashcards.q: What is goods-to-person, and why did it win in warehouse robotics?
flashcards.a: Instead of workers walking aisles to items, robots carry whole shelves to stationary pickers. It eliminates the largest labor cost (walking time), allows denser storage since humans never enter the grid, and turns fulfillment into a routing-optimization problem machines are good at.

flashcards.q: What does fleet orchestration do in a robotic warehouse?
flashcards.a: It's the real-time traffic-control layer assigning tasks and routes so thousands of robots share one floor without gridlock. The intelligence lives in this central optimization system more than in any individual robot — closer to air-traffic control than to a smart machine.

flashcards.q: Why does segment reporting matter more than company-wide results for a conglomerate?
flashcards.a: The blended average hides which business earns the money: a 35-40% margin cloud can sit inside a 3-5% margin retailer. Segment operating margins reveal the true engine, and sum-of-the-parts valuation — pricing each segment as a standalone company — follows directly from them.
